fields.value: Summons an invisible aerial servant to retrieve a described object or creature it can physically carry. It is a fetcher rather than an ordinary combat ally.
Caster needs protection from evil, a suitable magic circle/triangle/pentagram, or an appropriate religious symbol/artifact/relic to control it; without protection it slays the summoner.

When sent on a mission, the servant attacks by complete surprise and gains 4 free melee rounds unless the creature involved can detect invisible objects; then roll 1d6: 1 = 1 free round, 2 = 2, 3 = 3, 4 = 4, and 5 or 6 = 0 (the opponent is not surprised). Each round, the servant rolls to hit; a hit means it grabbed the assigned object or creature. If a creature is involved, compare strength; if it has no strength rating, roll the appropriate number and type of hit dice for the servant and creature. The higher total is the stronger.
The Monster Manual (p. 6) says the aerial servant can carry weights in excess of 10,000 gold pieces; this is a weight capacity, not a coin allowance.
Ends on completion, release, dispelling, expiry or the cleric’s death. Interference with its mission can have dangerous consequences.

fields.value: 1 cubic foot of solid material per level
Animates one or more objects to attack the initially designated target. Any material can be animated.

Movement depends on means of propulsion and weight. Examples: a large stone pedestal rocks forward 1″ per round, a stone statue moves 4″ per round, a wooden statue 8″ per round, and a light ivory stool 12″ per round; slithering is about 1″–2″ per round and rolling 3″–6″ per round.

Light, supple objects can only obscure vision, obstruct movement, bind, trip or smother. Light, hard objects can strike for 1–2 hit points or possibly obstruct and trip as light, supple objects; hard medium-weight objects can crush or strike for 2–8 hit points, and larger/heavier objects for 3–12, 4–16 or 5–20 hit points.

Attack frequency depends on locomotion, appendages and method of attack, ranging from once every five melee rounds to once per melee round. A hand-drawn protection has a 20% base escape chance. An inlaid or carved design has a 10% base chance, tested only initially to establish whether it was made properly. Modify the chance by the difference between caster intelligence plus experience level and captive intelligence plus level or hit dice: subtract a caster advantage, add a captive advantage.

Special pigments costing 1,000 gp per turn of preparation reduce a hand-made design's base chance by 1% per turn, to zero before the intelligence/level adjustment. Improving a permanent design to zero base chance takes at least one full month and at least 50,000 gp beyond its ordinary cost.

The DM rates a bribe, promise, or threat from 0 to 6 and subtracts that rating from the captive's intelligence. A roll at or below its adjusted intelligence refuses service. Offers can be renewed after 24 hours; confinement reduces intelligence by 1 for each such day.
Any break or blur in the protective inscription releases the captive automatically; even a straw crossing a line ruins it. The captive cannot itself place an object across the magical barrier.
Impossible or unreasonable commands are never accepted. A released creature may seek revenge.

Imprisons a lower-planar creature already held inside a restraining diagram. Choose one of six forms.
Chaining confines it with restraints that produce antipathy toward approaching creatures other than the caster; it lasts up to one year per effective caster level.
Slumber produces coma for up to one year per effective caster level. Bound slumber combines coma and chaining for up to one month per effective caster level.
Hedged prison confines it within an area until the magical hedge is broken. Metamorphosis makes all but its face or head noncorporeal until a prescribed freeing act.

No save applies if effective caster level is at least twice the subject's hit dice. Otherwise it receives a modified spell save; success frees it.
At most six magic-users can assist. Each assistant of 9th level or above adds one-third of that assistant's level; each assistant of levels 4–8 adds one level.
Chaining uses the ordinary save; slumber grants +1, bound slumber +2, hedged prison +3, metamorphosis +4, minimus containment +5.
Prior dolor imposes −1, prior torment −2, and the two used successively −4 on the save.

The first three forms can be renewed. After one year the captive gains a normal spell save and breaks free on success; interference that weakens chaining or slumber can also permit a normal save on renewal.
The first three forms keep the subject within its restraining diagram.

Add 1% per experience level and cumulative Intelligence bonuses above 12: 13–18 give +1%, +3%, +6%, +10%, +15%, +21% respectively. Treat monsters as the most applicable class. Spell-users use the detection-of-invisibility table instead.

Generate abilities using the method your DM permits, then choose race, class and alignment and record languages, money, equipment and hit points.
Keep a character record with possessions, spells and cumulative XP.
Race and class eligibility must be checked before choices are finalized.
Strength, intelligence, wisdom, dexterity, constitution and charisma describe different capabilities. The DM chooses the method used to generate them.
Ability requirements can restrict race or class choices.
Consult each ability's own adjustments rather than applying a universal modifier.
Strength affects melee accuracy, damage, carrying allowance and forcing obstacles. Fighters with strength 18 roll percentile dice for exceptional strength.
The exceptional-strength table is restricted to fighters in this PHB rule.
Fighters with strength 16 or higher receive a 10% earned-XP bonus.

Weight allowance adjusts the normal unencumbered allowance, measured in gold-piece weight (10 gp = 1 lb). Parenthesized door chances are out of six for fighters forcing locked, barred, magically held or wizard-locked doors: only one attempt per door is allowed. Bend-bars/lift-gates attempts are also one-time attempts.

fields.value: Intelligence limits a magic-user's spell levels and spells known. Learning checks use percentile dice against the applicable chance-to-know entry.
A successful check determines whether the spell can be learned when found.
The minimum-spells rule permits rechecking failed spells until the minimum is met.
Stop learning in that spell-level group when the maximum is reached.
Additional languages by Intelligence: 3–7: 0; 8–9: 1; 10–11: 2; 12–13: 3; 14–15: 4; 16: 5; 17: 6; 18: 7. Nonhuman language rules and racial limits also apply.

Magic-user spell learning rows are Intelligence: chance to know each listed spell / minimum spells per spell level / maximum spells per spell level: 9: 35%/4/6; 10–12: 45%/5/7; 13–14: 55%/6/9; 15–16: 65%/7/11; 17: 75%/8/14; 18: 85%/9/18; 19 or more: 95%/10/all.
Minimum Intelligence to use magic-user spells of levels 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 is respectively 10, 12, 14, 16 and 18.

fields.value: Wisdom's clerical bonus spells are cumulative, but become available only when the cleric can already cast that spell level. Low wisdom can cause spell failure.
The magical-attack adjustment applies to mental attacks involving willpower, not every saving throw.
A failed clerical spell is expended with no effect.
Magical-attack saving-throw adjustment by Wisdom: 3 −3; 4 −2; 5–7 −1; 8–14 none; 15 +1; 16 +2; 17 +3; 18 +4. This applies to mental attack forms involving will force.

Cleric bonus spell increments and failure chance by Wisdom: 9 none/20%; 10 none/15%; 11 none/10%; 12 none/5%; 13 one 1st-level/0%; 14 one 1st-level/0%; 15 one 2nd-level/0%; 16 one 2nd-level/0%; 17 one 3rd-level/0%; 18 one 4th-level/0%. fields.value: Apply the constitution hit-point adjustment to each hit die; a penalty cannot reduce a die below 1 hit point.
Under this PHB rule, only fighters, including paladins and rangers, receive constitution bonuses above +2 per die.
System shock and resurrection survival are different percentage checks.

The initial Constitution score caps the number of raise-dead or resurrection revivifications, and each such revivification reduces Constitution by 1. Increasing or restoring Constitution does not raise that original limit. The text notes that other magic such as wish may provide another means.

fields.value: The PHB offers dwarf, elf, gnome, half-elf, halfling, half-orc and human characters. Racial tables restrict classes and, for many non-human classes, advancement.
Your DM may restrict available races for the campaign.
UA provides additional racial choices and revised limits; keep the selected source explicit.

PHB class level table (U = unlimited; parenthesized entries are non-player characters only; omitted classes are unavailable to that race): dwarf fighter 9, thief U, assassin 9, cleric (8); elf fighter 7, magic-user 11, thief U, assassin 10, cleric (7); gnome fighter 6, illusionist 7, thief U, assassin 8, cleric (7); half-elf cleric 5, druid U, fighter 8, ranger 8, magic-user 8, thief U, assassin 11; halfling fighter 6, thief U, druid (6); half-orc cleric 4, fighter 10, thief 8, assassin U; human all listed classes U. All are still subject to applicable ability and class requirements.

PHB fighter limits by Strength: dwarf below 17 → 7, at 17 → 8, otherwise maximum 9; elf below 17 → 5, at 17 → 6, otherwise maximum 7; gnome below 18 → 5, otherwise 6; half-elf below 17 → 6, at 17 → 7, otherwise 8. Halfling Hairfeet and others under Strength 17 → 4; Tallfellows at 17 and Stouts at 18 → 5; Tallfellows with 18 → 6.

PHB magic-user limits by Intelligence: elf below 17 → 9, at 17 → 10, otherwise maximum 11; half-elf below 17 → 6, at 17 → 7, otherwise maximum 8. Gnome illusionists with Intelligence or Dexterity below 17 are limited to 5; with both 17 to 6; otherwise table maximum 7. Half-orc thieves with Dexterity below 17 are limited to 6, at 17 to 7, otherwise maximum 8.
The printed half-elven ranger 8 entry bears footnote 4, but that footnote explicitly describes half-elven fighters. The table’s application of that footnote to rangers is unresolved.

fields.value: A human may stop advancing in one profession and begin another, subject to ability and alignment requirements. This differs from simultaneous non-human multiclassing.
Required principal abilities are at least 15 in the original class and 17 in the new class.
Using the former class's functions before surpassing its level forfeits XP for that adventure.
Once the new level exceeds the old, class functions may be combined subject to equipment restrictions.
Alignment combines attitudes to law and chaos with good and evil. Some classes require a specific alignment or a limited set of alignments.
A paladin is lawful good; a druid is true neutral under these PHB rules.
Actual behavior can differ from the character's declared alignment.
Voluntary alignment changes can require sacrifices, acts or quests at the DM's discretion. Returning to a discarded alignment is especially difficult.
The DM tracks the effects of the character's behavior.
Do not treat alignment as a freely changeable label.
Hit points combine physical resilience with skill, luck and supernatural protection. Restoring lost points cannot raise the character beyond their established total.
Hit-die type and exceptional starting dice depend on class.
Record current and maximum hit points separately.
A character must find a speaker and remain near the instructor. The stated study period is one year, reduced by one month for each intelligence point above 12.
Study only one new language at a time.
The campaign determines which languages and instructors are available.
One gold piece equals 20 silver pieces, 200 copper pieces or 2 electrum pieces. One platinum piece equals 5 gold pieces.
Coin denominations are assumed to have similar size and weight.
Money changers typically charge 3% for an exchange.
Plan purchases around both available funds and encumbrance. The campaign may require visiting several sellers, and availability and prices can vary.
Record where important equipment is carried so it can be reached when needed.
Armor and shields establish a base AC, with dexterity and magic modifying it. Lower numeric armor classes offer better protection.
Unarmored is AC 10; plate mail with a shield is AC 2 in this table.
Each +1 of magic armor or shield decreases AC by 1.
A monster's AC may represent hide, agility or other defenses rather than worn armor.
Base AC without shield: leather or padded 8; studded leather or ring mail 7; scale 6; chain 5; splint or banded 4; plate 3.
A shield improves these listed armor classes by one when applicable; shield alone is AC 9.

fields.value: Shield protection assumes the wearer can interpose it against the attack. This PHB rule limits how many attacks it covers in a melee round.
Small shield: one attack; normal shield: two; large shield: three.
Attacks from the right flank or rear negate the shield benefit.

A proficiency covers the magical version of the same weapon type.
Apply the class's non-proficiency penalty to the attack roll.
Class entries are initial proficiencies / non-proficiency penalty / levels above 1st per added proficiency.
Magic-user and illusionist each 1 / −5 / 6; thief 2 / −3 / 4; assassin 3 / −2 / 4; monk 1 / −3 / 2.

fields.value: The weapon table's armor-class adjustments assume short range. Medium range applies a further −2 and long range a further −5.
Use the appropriate weapon's listed range bands.
The table also distinguishes rate of fire from individual weapon damage.
Hireling recruitment depends on local availability and the offered wages and benefits. The DM determines local hiring terms.
Charisma does not cap the number of ordinary hirelings.
Employment can be arranged for different periods by agreement.
Henchmen are NPC adventurers supported by a patron. They require upkeep and an appropriate share of treasure, and their loyalty depends on treatment as well as charisma.
Their XP is usually about half the amount their participation and treasure share would otherwise yield, and can be less.
A dungeon turn is 10 minutes, a melee round is 1 minute, and a segment is 6 seconds.
There are 10 rounds per turn and 10 segments per round.
Track elapsed time for light, spells, travel, recovery and upkeep.
The inch notation generally means 10 feet indoors and 10 yards outdoors for range. Spell areas do not automatically triple outdoors.
Outdoor range scaling must not be applied to a spell's area of effect.

fields.value: Exploration and map-making slow dungeon travel. Light, probing tools, ropes and a reliable record of the route are practical expedition needs.
Plan how the group will return and carry recovered treasure.
Carrying limits depend on weight and bulk, not weight alone. Heavy loads reduce movement and can worsen reaction or initiative.
Ten gold pieces of weight equal one pound in this system.
Consider whether carried equipment is accessible.
During mapping and exploration, each inch of movement rate gives 10 feet per 10-minute turn. Following a known route is five times as fast.
Flight or combat movement is normally ten times the exploration pace, except for the encumbered case.
Fast pursuit or escape does not permit mapping.
A movement rate of 12 inches corresponds to 120 feet per combat round.

Track remaining fuel and elapsed turns.
A bullseye lantern illuminates 80 feet in a 1-inch-wide beam which can be shuttered; one pint of fine oil burns for 24 turns.
The table lists infinite illumination for a magic dagger at 10 feet, magic short sword at 15 feet, and magic long sword at 20 feet.

fields.value: The usual initiative check rolls a d6 for each side each round; the higher score normally acts first. Surprise, haste, slow and detailed combat cases can change the sequence.
Dexterity is not a universal initiative modifier.
Consult DMG combat procedures for ties, multiple attack routines and spell-versus-weapon timing.
A saving throw may avoid an effect or reduce its consequences. The required score depends on the saving-throw category, class and level, with relevant adjustments.
Individual spells specify what a successful save does.
Items can require separate saves against destructive effects.
Attack rolls instead use the applicable attack matrix and target AC.
This PHB passage uses 1d6 damage per 10 feet fallen, to a maximum of 20d6, with surface-related adjustments left to the referee.
This card reports the supplied PHB text; later interpretations or errata require a separate citation.
Establish surprise and distance, determine initiative when applicable, then resolve the sides' chosen actions. Repeat distance, initiative and action while the encounter continues.
Actions may include avoiding contact, parley, missiles, spells, closing, charging or melee.
A minute-long melee round represents maneuvering and unsuccessful attempts as well as scored blows.

A tied initiative result normally resolves attacks simultaneously, so both sides can inflict damage. In weapon-versus-weapon melee, compare weapon speed factors instead: the lower factor strikes first.
A large weapon-speed difference can permit additional attacks under the DMG procedure.
Multiple attack routines and charges have their own ordering rules.
When actions are not simultaneous, incapacitation can prevent an opponent from completing its action.

76–95: friendly, immediate action; 96–00 or greater: enthusiastically friendly, immediate acceptance.

fields.value: Declare the spell before initiative is known. Casting must be continuous and requires concentration; a successful interrupting attack spoils and expends it.
The caster cannot dodge with a dexterity defense bonus while continuing to cast.
Running, ordinary walking or interrupting the gestures prevents completion.
Completion depends on casting time and the detailed initiative procedure.
A cleric normally has one turning attempt, but successful attempts against a mixed group can continue on later rounds against other types until an attempt fails.
Turning generally proceeds from the lower-hit-die types to higher types.
The DM may apply the stated exception for lesser undead serving an unaffected greater undead.
Hard cover can improve applicable saving throws. With at least 90% cover, a successful appropriate save can prevent all damage.
Apply the actual cover and spell circumstances.
This is a cover rule, not a universal result for every successful save.
Morale checks can govern non-leader NPCs, hirelings, henchmen and intelligent opponents. Casualties, lost leadership and superior enemy force can trigger checks.

Check each round against an obviously superior force. Apply +5% at 25% party casualties, +10% if the leader is unconscious, +15% at 50% or more casualties, and +30% if the leader is slain or deserts; the casualty thresholds also apply to individual wounds.

Modifiers: each enemy deserting −5%, each enemy slain −10%, inflicting casualties without receiving any −20%, each friend killed +10%, taking casualties without inflicting any +10%, each friend deserting +15%, and being outnumbered and outclassed at least 3 to 1 +20%.
Roll percentile dice against the creature’s morale or loyalty score after adjustments; the amount by which the adjusted roll exceeds the score determines the failure outcome.
Failure by 1–15% means fall back fighting; 16–30% disengage and retreat; 31–50% flee in panic; 51% or more surrender.

fields.value: For eligible creatures, subduing blows use the nonlethal parts of weapons. Unless a specific rule says otherwise, 75% of subdual damage is temporary and 25% is real.
This procedure does not apply to player characters.
Eligibility and creature-specific rules still need to be checked.
Complete rest restores 1 hit point per day in the first week. Constitution modifies weekly recovery, and four continuous weeks restore full hit points.
A negative constitution adjustment removes that many healing days from each week's recovery.
After the first week, add the constitution bonus to each week's healing.
Combat, spellcasting and similar activity do not count as rest.
At 0 hit points a creature becomes unconscious under this DMG procedure, then loses 1 point per following round until death at −10. Immediate aid stops that continuing loss.
The text optionally allows the triggering blow to leave the creature as low as −3.
After revival: 1d6 turns of coma and at least one week of rest; ordinary cures do not remove the restriction, but heal does.
More severe negative totals can have lasting consequences at the DM's option.
The DM weighs the challenge against the participating characters' power before determining XP awards. Outwitting guards and overcoming traps can also qualify.
The award procedure is not simply a fixed reward for every encounter.
Treasure must be removed from the dungeon or lair and converted to a transportable form or stored safely to count for experience.
Gold-equivalent treasure can award 1 XP per gp when the challenge warrants it; weaker guardians reduce the ratio.
Items sold before XP is awarded contribute their sale proceeds to treasure taken.
Retained magic items receive their smaller listed XP value rather than sale value.
The suggested method divides monster XP equally among surviving participants, with adjustments for challenge and henchman status.
A genuinely single-handed kill can be credited separately.
A caster protected by allies is not acting single-handedly.
Reaching an XP threshold does not automatically grant the next level. The DM assesses performance and the required period of training or study.
The assessment ordinarily determines 1–4 weeks of training.
Below name level, standard weekly cost is the current level × 1,500 gp.
Do not treat the next level's benefits as available before training is completed.
Initial training normally requires a tutor of the same class and profession. A performance score below 2 permits self-training at twice the time.

At name level, characters train or study independently for the performance-determined time; weekly cost per level is 2,000 gp for clerics, 1,000 for fighters, 4,000 for magic-users, and 2,000 for thieves.
Training must be continuous; serious interruption loses the prior time and payment.
Once eligible to advance, further XP cannot be accumulated until the new level is actually acquired.

Bards contribute at least 50% of monetary gains plus 1,000 gp per level upon advancement to their college, through a druid able to use more of their highest-level spells than the bard; failure to pay prevents advancement. They otherwise need one week of study or training upon gaining sufficient XP.

fields.value: UA adds comeliness for physical appearance and initial reactions. Charisma still governs the longer-term interpersonal relationship once a character is known.

Roll 3d6 for base comeliness after the first six abilities. Charisma modifiers: below 3 −8; 3 −5; 4–5 −3; 6–8 −1; 9–12 0; 13–15 +1; 16–17 +2; 18 +3; above 18 +5. Later gains or losses of charisma adjust comeliness point for point.

Racial adjustment applies to reactions from other races: half-orc −3; dwarf or gnome −1; halfling or human 0; half-elf or sylvan elf +1; gray or high elf +2. Treat each starred pair as the same race for this purpose.

The following reaction bands concern creatures of human sort. At −16 or below, viewers recoil, flee or may attack; if viewer and subject are both evil, treat the score as positive. At −15 to −9, viewers show disgust and hostility; if all are evil, the negative score can be regarded as positive. At −8 to 0, viewers feel aversion and may become openly hostile.

At 1–6, viewers tend toward unease; enough conversation can let charisma offset it. At 7–9, the initial reaction is negative but high charisma can quickly overcome it. At 10–13, appearance has no effect on the viewer.
At 14–17, initial reaction improves by a percentage equal to the score; members of the opposite sex are affected as by fascination unless their Wisdom exceeds half the score.

At 18–21, initial reaction improves by 150% of the score. Opposite-sex viewers are affected as by fascination unless Wisdom exceeds two-thirds the score; same-sex viewers are similarly affected unless Wisdom is at least half the score. Harsh rejection can cause the rejected individual to react as if the subject had negative comeliness equal to half the positive score.

At 22–25, the reaction adjustment is twice the score. Fascination affects those with Wisdom less than two-thirds of the score; a consciously sought opposite-sex individual is fascinated unless Wisdom is 18 or higher. Harsh rejection has the same effect as in the 18–21 band.

At 26–30, reserved for unusual extraplanar demigods or deities, the reaction adjustment is twice the score. Fascination applies except to those with Wisdom at least 75% of the score, and Wisdom 19 or higher always permits a saving throw. A consciously sought opposite-sex individual is affected unless Wisdom is 20 or higher.

Fascination allows a saving throw versus spell; nonmagical comeliness fascination is not removed by dispel magic or antimagic. A fascinated creature follows an order if 3d6 does not exceed the subject’s comeliness: add 1 to the roll for requests against its interest, up to +6 or more for hazardous requests; a higher roll breaks fascination. Treatment during fascination affects subsequent reaction.

Comeliness is temporary as a reaction factor: once the subject is known, use charisma. Fascination does not prevent fighting or spellcasting or make the subject a puppet. Change self and alter self adjust comeliness by at most 1 point; an illusion of a high-comeliness creature works for one round; polymorph changes it by 2 points; shapechange gives the final form’s full effect.

fields.value: Fighters and rangers can choose weapon specialization at creation. It normally uses two proficiency slots; a non-crossbow bow requires an additional slot.

Only fighters and rangers may specialize, choosing at character creation. Specialization costs two proficiency slots; a non-crossbow bow requires one additional slot. The weapon must be a specific type.
Melee specialization grants +1 to hit and +2 damage in addition to applicable Strength and magic bonuses. Other missile weapons also grant +1 to hit and +2 damage.

Bow point blank is 6–30 feet: +2 to hit and damage and double damage on a hit; the source gives 6–16 damage for a nonmagical arrow, plus applicable Strength or magic bonuses. At short range, beginning at 30 feet up to the lower limit of medium range, the specialist gains +1 to hit and damage. A nocked and drawn bow with target in sight may fire before initiative.

Crossbow point blank is 6–60 feet: +2 to hit and damage and double damage, with a 6–12 nonmagical light-crossbow example excluding Strength or magic bonuses. At short range gain +1 to hit and damage; at medium gain +1 to hit with no specialization damage bonus. A cocked and aimed crossbow with target in range gains a shot before initiative.

Specialist attacks per round at levels 1–6 / 7–12 / 13+: melee 3/2, 2/1, 5/2; bow 2/1, 3/1, 4/1; light crossbow 1/1, 3/2, 2/1; heavy crossbow 1/2, 1/1, 3/2; lasso or staff sling 1/1, 3/2, 2/1; thrown dagger 3/1, 4/1, 5/1; thrown dart 4/1, 5/1, 6/1; other missiles or hurled weapons 3/2, 2/1, 5/2. The table supersedes ordinary fighter/ranger attacks for the specialized weapon.

Double specialization costs another proficiency slot when a character qualifies for a new weapon, and must be in the weapon already specialized in. Only melee weapons qualify, excluding pole arms and the two-handed sword; it gives +3 to hit and +3 damage with that weapon.
Specialization hit bonuses are not magical and do not affect creatures hit only by magical weapons; applicable magical weapon bonuses are additional.

Restoring each point of absorption costs 100 gp and one day with a trained armorer.

A buckler protects against one chosen opponent in a melee round and can be strapped to the arm for use by crossbowmen or slingers.
For a small demi-human such as a gnome or halfling it is treated as a small shield.
A non-human or part-human character must meet the race's ability minimums. Apply racial bonuses and penalties before enforcing the race's maximum scores.

The source gives +1 per 3½ constitution points; it is not a blanket bonus to every saving throw.

fields.value: A dwarf actively inspecting nearby stonework can detect a slope or new construction at 75%, sliding walls at 4 in 6 and stonework traps at 50%.
The phenomenon must normally be within 10 feet.
Approximate underground depth can be determined at 50%, without the 10-foot restriction.
These facts do not appear automatically: the character must deliberately seek them.
Dwarves add +1 to melee attacks against half-orcs, goblins, hobgoblins and orcs. Certain much larger enemies suffer −4 on their attacks against the dwarf.
The larger-enemy list is ogres, trolls, ogre magi, giants and titans.
Do not extend these named racial advantages to every small or large opponent.
PHB elves resist sleep and charm spells 90% of the time. If charm passes that resistance, its ordinary saving throw still applies.
Elves add +1 to attack rolls with a short sword, long sword or any bow other than a crossbow.
The PHB elf is a high elf; UA sub-races can change these traits.
An elf or half-elf passing within 10 feet of a concealed door has a 1-in-6 chance to notice it. Deliberate searching gives better chances.
An active search finds a secret door on 2 in 6.
An active search finds a concealed door on 3 in 6.
Secret and concealed doors are separate cases in this rule.
An elf not wearing metal armor can gain a 4-in-6 surprise chance when alone, with suitable elven or halfling company, or at least 90 feet ahead of a mixed party.
If a door or other portal must be opened to confront the target, the chance drops to 2 in 6.
Apply the stated party composition, distance and armor conditions rather than treating this as universal surprise.
Gnomes receive constitution-based saving bonuses against rods, staves, wands and spells. Their PHB racial description does not give the dwarven poison bonus.
In melee, add +1 to hit kobolds or goblins.
Gnolls, bugbears, ogres, trolls, ogre magi, giants and titans suffer −4 on attacks against a gnome.
Do not confuse a saving-throw bonus with a percentage magic-resistance ability.
An actively concentrating gnome can detect a passage slope at 80%, unsafe stonework at 70%, approximate depth at 60% and direction of travel at 50%.
Slope and unsafe-stonework checks require the area to be within 10 feet.
Approximate underground depth can be checked without the 10-foot restriction.
The ability must be used deliberately; it is not automatic awareness.
Half-elves have 60-foot infravision and 30% resistance to sleep and charm spells. Charm still allows its normal save if it gets past the racial resistance.
Their secret- and concealed-door chances match those described for elves.
Only intelligence above 16 adds to their listed starting languages: one at 17 or two at 18.
Halflings gain constitution-based bonuses against rods, staves, wands, spells and poisons.
Halfling infravision varies with ancestry: mixed blood is described as 30 feet, pure stout as 60 feet.
The racial ability adjustment is −1 strength and +1 dexterity.
A halfling not in metal armor can surprise on 4 in 6 when alone or sufficiently ahead of an unsuitable mixed party; opening a door reduces this to 2 in 6.
The stated advance distance is at least 90 feet.
The source's compatible company is halflings or elves not wearing metal armor.
Stout or mixed-stock underground detection also requires concentration.
Half-orcs add +1 to initial strength and constitution. Their −2 charisma adjustment applies to non-half-orc NPC henchmen, so retain the unadjusted score for those of their own race.
Record the unadjusted charisma as well for dealings with half-orcs.
In addition to common, alignment language and orcish, they may learn at most two further languages.
Humans receive no racial ability bonuses or penalties and have no racial restriction on class choice or maximum level.
Class ability, alignment and class-specific limits still apply.
The human procedure for changing professions is distinct from non-human simultaneous multiclassing.
A non-human multiclass character divides earned experience equally among the chosen classes, including a class in which the racial level limit has already been reached.
Do not redirect the capped class's share to the other class or classes.

Required complete rest depends on the highest-level spell to be recovered, not on how many spells are missing.
Spell levels 1–2: 4 hours; 3–4: 6 hours; 5–6: 8 hours; 7–8: 10 hours; 9: 12 hours.

fields.value: UA elven sub-races retain many high-elf traits but add specific changes. Gray elves gain +1 intelligence, potentially reaching 19.

Gray elves share high-elf abilities, including sleep and charm resistance, sword and bow ability, infravision, secret/concealed-door detection and silent movement when alone. They share high-elf languages and add +1 to the initial Intelligence roll, up to 19.

Wood (sylvan) elves have similar elven traits, gain +1 initial Strength (maximum 18) and −1 initial Intelligence. Their starting languages are elvish, common, treant and the tongue of woodland mammals; the passage gives them no other starting languages.

Wild elves (grugach) retain standard elven resistance, weapon bonuses, infravision, silent movement and door detection. They gain +2 initial Strength (maximum 18), deal with woodland creatures as if animal friendship were in effect, and set pits, snares and natural traps with a 90% success chance. Most speak only elvish, though a player character may also know some common.

The UA p.7 class table permits gray elves to be cavaliers, clerics, druids, fighters, rangers, magic-users or thieves (including acrobats and assassins); wood elves have those choices except cavalier; wild elves can be druids, fighters or thieves (including acrobats and assassins). Wild elf multiclassing is restricted to fighter/thief.
These are the UA class choices; ability requirements, multiclass rules and the separate UA class-level limits still apply. Do not merge them with the PHB-only class limits.

UA level-limit table conventions: use Wisdom for cleric/druid, Strength for fighter/ranger/assassin, Intelligence for magic-user, and Dexterity for thief; additional ability requirements appear in footnotes. U means unlimited for the appropriate race/class, subject to the highest level attainable by the class. Below the first score shown, use the lowest listed level; scores above the table do not raise its maximum. If single-classed and that class is an available multiclass choice for the character, the limit may be exceeded by 2. Class eligibility still applies.
UA elf cleric (all except dark elves): Wisdom 12–15: 7; 16: 8; 17: 9; 18: 10; 19: 11; 20–21: 12. Wild elves are not eligible for cleric under UA p.7.

UA elf druid: wild elf Wisdom 12–17: 10; 18: 11 and 19: 12, both requiring Charisma 18; 20: 14 and 21: 17, both requiring Charisma 19. The 12–17 rows have no additional Charisma footnote; normal class requirements still apply. Other elves: U, where class-eligible.

UA elf fighter: Strength 12–17 gives gray/high 5, wild 7, wood 6; 18 gives 6/8/7; 18/75 gives 7/8/8; 18/90 gives 8/10/9; 18/99 gives 9/11/10; 18/00 gives 10/12/11; 19 gives 11/13/12; 20 gives 11/13/14. Values in each group are gray/high, wild, wood respectively.

fields.value: The DMG offers several alternatives to straight 3d6 ability generation; the DM selects the campaign's method.
Method I: roll 4d6 for each ability score, discard the lowest die, then arrange the six scores.
Method II: roll 3d6 twelve times, keep the highest six totals, then arrange them.
Methods III and IV retain the normal ability order rather than letting a player freely rearrange scores.
Method III: for each of Strength, Intelligence, Wisdom, Dexterity, Constitution and Charisma, roll 3d6 six times and keep that ability's highest total.
Method IV: generate twelve complete, ordered sets of six scores with 3d6; select one entire set.

A campaign may assign a secondary trade or craft to player characters and, if desired, henchmen. Assign it randomly or select it to suit the campaign's background. The skill gives limited practical knowledge judged by the DM.
An armorer might judge the quality of normal armor, repair chain links, or perhaps fashion certain weapons.
This procedure does not supply a universal proficiency-check system.
Random percentile: 01–02 armorer; 03–04 bowyer/fletcher; 05–10 farmer/gardener; 11–14 fisher (netting); 15–20 forester; 21–23 gambler; 24–27 hunter/fisher (hook and line).

28–32 husbandman (animal husbandry); 33–34 jeweler/lapidary; 35–37 leather worker/tanner; 38–39 limner/painter; 40–42 mason/carpenter; 43–44 miner; 45–46 navigator (fresh or salt water); 47–49 sailor (fresh or salt); 50–51 shipwright (boats or ships).

52–54 tailor/weaver; 55–57 teamster/freighter; 58–60 trader/barterer; 61–64 trapper/furrier; 65–67 woodworker/cabinetmaker; 68–85 no skill of measurable worth; 86–00 roll twice, ignoring that result thereafter.
At 1st level, the class is assumed to have been the character's main prior profession. Secondary skills reflect minor mundane training picked up earlier or incidentally.

The prose says to roll to determine whether a second skill is known and, on a 'TWO SKILLS' result, assign an appropriate second skill. The 86–00 table entry is worded 'ROLL TWICE IGNORING THIS RESULT HEREAFTER'.
Other examples of secondary-skill use include judging an item's general worth and soundness, finding food, making small repairs, and constructing crude items. These are examples for DM adjudication.
To judge a skill's extent, consider what someone who knows only a little about the subject could do; use that as a scale for the character's secondary skill.

An encounter occurs on 1: use d20 in densely populated country, d12 in moderately to sparsely populated or patrolled areas, and d10 in wilderness.

fields.value: The aerial damage procedure ties continued flight to how much damage a winged creature has taken.
More than 50% damage prevents maintaining flight and requires landing; more than 75% prevents a controlled descent.

That allowance does not add real hit points or prevent death.

The maximum vessel speeds are burst rates, not sustainable daily travel rates.
Account for crew rest when planning a voyage or chase.
A vessel's hull value measures the damage it can take before sinking. Repairs become necessary when damage reaches one-third of that value.
Damage from one-third through one-half of hull value can be repaired at sea.
Damage beyond one-half requires reaching port for repairs.
Ships can use grapnels and lines to draw alongside for boarding, while the defending crew can try to cut them free.

The basic underwater sight limits are 50 feet in fresh water and 100 feet in salt water, adjusted for available light, depth and obstructions.
Seaweed, fish and stirred sediment can obscure or completely block the view.
Combat on a muddy bottom can leave vision blocked while the motion continues and for 7–12 rounds afterward, unless a current clears it.
Water resistance prevents effective ordinary use of crushing and cleaving weapons; thrusting weapons remain useful.
Aquatic opponents normally strike before land-born combatants unless the latter have a significantly longer weapon.
Free action removes this reaction disadvantage and permits ordinary weapon use.
An underwater combat net requires special training; an untrained character attacks with it at −4.

Center the sphere on the point from which the bolt would normally originate.

Ordinary infravision distinguishes temperature differences; objects at the same temperature can blend together.
A heat-producing light source interferes with normal infravision.
Readjusting after ordinary vision takes at least two segments.
A sufficiently warm creature can leave thermal footprints detectable for two rounds.
Ultravision helps outdoors under appropriate sky conditions, but it does not supply its own light underground.

If the pursued are faster, pursuit ends when they are visible over 100 feet away, leave sight over 50 feet away, or pursuit exceeds 5 rounds without perceptible gain.
At equal speed, the respective limits are over 150 feet visible, over 80 feet when leaving sight, or over 1 turn without perceptible gain.
If pursuers are faster, pursuit ends only when the pursued leave sight over 200 feet away or the pursuers cannot continue for endurance reasons.
Special tracking senses can defeat ordinary attempts to escape; mapping and measured navigation are not available while fleeing.

At a three-way choice without sight, sound or scent clues, a pursuer has a two-in-three chance of taking the wrong way.

For palatable food or wine offered to pursuers of low intelligence or less, determine a 10%–100% base chance with d10 unless their hunger is known; add 10% per intelligence point below 5. Test with a second d10; success lasts one round or the time needed to collect the treasure, whichever is longer. Tiny valuables can go unnoticed.

fields.value: Flank attacks negate the defender's shield AC benefit. Rear-flank attacks also remove the dexterity AC bonus.
An attack directly from the rear gains +2 to hit and ignores both shield and dexterity AC benefits.
Stunned, prone or motionless opponents are attacked on that rear-attack basis, with +4 to hit instead of +2.

When the attacker remains exposed to enemy actions in general melee, weapon attacks that can affect a magically sleeping or held opponent hit automatically for maximum damage, with twice the usual attack routines.
Outside general melee, one such helpless creature can be bound or killed per round.
These special provisions do not automatically apply to an ordinarily sleeping creature.
A character normally fighting with one weapon may use a dagger or hand axe in the other hand. The baseline penalties are −2 with the primary weapon and −4 with the secondary.

At the start of a round, players should state what their characters are attempting precisely enough to resolve timing.
Retrieving an item, moving and using it can be separate actions; a sequence may take more than one round.
A changed plan starts from the character's current position and progress, rather than resetting the round.

04–08: Nausea and −1 strength and dexterity for 5–20 rounds, no save; one potion is cancelled and the other has half strength and duration, determined randomly.
09–15: Both potions are cancelled. 16–25: One randomly selected potion is cancelled and the other remains normal. 26–35: Both are at half efficacy.

36–90: Both work normally unless contradictory effects cancel. 91–99: One randomly selected potion has 150% efficacy, subject to the DM deciding whether effect and duration or only duration may increase.
00: One potion functions permanently on the imbiber; harmful side effects are possible.

Greater mistletoe is properly harvested by the druid: on Midsummer’s Eve, locate it, cut it with a gold or silver sickle, and catch it in a bowl before it touches the ground.
Lesser mistletoe was not harvested on the eve of Midsummer, or was taken in an unprescribed way such as picking it by hand.
Borrowed mistletoe is mistletoe not personally harvested by the druid.
Holly and oak leaves must be gathered by the druid, but may be picked or gathered in any manner.

PHB p. 30: open-hand attacks can stun or kill. A stun requires a hit roll at least 5 above the minimum required and lasts 1–6 melee rounds. Killing is a separate percentile roll: the monk must first hit and stun, then roll equal to or below the opponent’s AC modified by the monk’s levels above 7; the source notes a negative chance at AC −1.

PHB p. 32: quivering palm is a separate ability, attempted only once per week; the monk must touch the intended victim within 3 melee rounds or the power is drained for one week. It has no effect on undead or creatures hit only by magical weapons; the victim cannot have more hit dice than the monk, and its hit points cannot exceed the monk’s by more than 200%. The death command must come within one day per monk level at use or the vibrations cease harmlessly. The general monk restriction is no Strength bonus to hit probability or damage.

fields.value: All 210 cells of matrix I.B were checked against the supplied revised December 1979 Dungeon Masters Guide scan.
The table applies to fighters, paladins, and rangers. Bards use their highest attained fighter level, not their current bard level. Its separate level-0 column applies to halflings and humans.

A cell is the table's 20-sided-die target for the named attacker level band and opponent armor class, before resolving applicable adjustments. It is not automatically equivalent to AC-zero target minus armor class.
The original table repeats 20 in some columns, so a single linear THAC0 subtraction can disagree with it. The examples below use only cells actually legible in this scan.
Any current group convention using simple THAC0 remains a group choice; this reference does not silently replace that convention or the printed matrix.
The matrix prints a −2 adjustment at medium missile range and −5 at long range.

The DM may choose a +1 to-hit bonus at the second level within each two-level fighter band, producing the source's optional per-level progression instead of the ordinary two-level steps. Do not silently apply this option.

For the listed kinds of spell effects, including curse, prayer, and protection from evil, the DMG instructs the referee to adjust the relevant armor class rather than reduce the attack die result. This preserves the intended repeated-20 behavior. This note is about those spell adjustments, not a universal conversion of every modifier into AC.
Repeated 20s and a separate natural-20 option

The DMG explains the repeated 20s as part of the printed combat-table progression. It then offers an optional amendment: second and later repeated-20 entries require a natural 20, and targets above 20 require a natural 20 plus sufficient bonus. The initial 20 entry still permits die result plus bonuses. Keep that amendment distinct from the unamended printed table; do not infer an unconditional natural-20 rule from it.
With no additional adjustments in this illustration, the original matrix's repeated 20 differs from the linear calculation 20 − (−1).
The source-listed cell is 20; a simple AC-zero subtraction would produce 24. No missing cells were generated from that formula.

These labels describe the progression represented by each guide. Check race, abilities, alignment, and campaign requirements in the cited rules before choosing a character’s classes.
PHB pp. 32–33 presents combinations operated at the same time by non-human or semi-human characters. The combinations available depend on race; this is a separate procedure from changing professions.

PHB p. 33’s human-only profession change stops advancement in the former class. It requires principal attribute scores of at least 15 in the original class and 17 or 18 in the new class, with alignment restrictions. The character retains earlier hit points but begins the new class’s other functions at level 1. Former-class functions restrict new-class XP until the new level exceeds the old one.

The bard appendix supplies a fighter → thief → bard sequence. UA supplies a thief-acrobat specialist path and an advanced druid track with an XP reset. Each follows its own cited transition rules; their labels do not grant general permission to combine classes.
“Dual-class” is a navigation gloss here. PHB p. 33 heads its sequential rule “The Character With Two Classes.”

The bard appendix permits humans and half-elves, while the general two-class rule requires a human. The bard guide is classified by its appendix sequence rather than automatically assigned that general procedure.
For the bard’s thief-stage transition, PHB p. 117 says “between 5th and 9th.” This metadata retains that wording without resolving its boundary convention.
UA p. 23 calls thief-acrobat a “split-class” specialist; UA p. 25 otherwise treats the specialist as a thief except for the stated changes.
A Class track badge identifies one guide’s advancement table; it makes no finding about eligibility for a permitted race-based class combination.

checkedValues./guidance/0: Requires Strength 15 and Dexterity 16, and five completed thief levels.
checkedValues./guidance/1: On qualifying for level 6, train for six weeks under a thief-acrobat of at least level 10.
checkedValues./guidance/2: Pick pockets, opening locks, and finding/removing traps stop improving at their level-5 ability; magical writing is never gained.
checkedValues./guidance/3: Use the specialist acrobatics tables and explicit climbing progression. UA pp.23 and 25 describe stopped, retained and generally inherited thief abilities; later progression of the four retained skills remains a campaign interpretation.
checkedValues./retainedSkillsNote: UA p.23 explicitly freezes pick pockets, opening locks, and finding/removing traps at fifth-level ability, and reading magical writings is never gained. It says the acrobat retains move silently, hide in shadows, hear noise, and read languages acquired through fifth level, while climb walls increases with experience level. UA p.25 generally treats the acrobat as a thief except as indicated. These passages do not expressly give a new progression for the four retained abilities; no categorical freeze or automatic increases are supplied here.
checkedValues./progression/description: After five ordinary thief levels, a character with Strength 15+ and Dexterity 16+ may specialize on qualifying for level 6. Training takes six weeks with a thief-acrobat of at least level 10. UA calls this a “split-class” specialist and otherwise treats it as a thief except for the stated changes; it has its own specialist advancement table.

checkedValues./description: UA extends the druid hierarchy through Grand Druid and a separate Hierophant progression. The XP reset makes a simple level-1 cumulative array unsuitable.
checkedValues./levelChanges/0/changes/0: Grand Druid eligibility begins at 3,000,001 XP; the office knows six spells of each spell level and gains the stated extra six spell levels, subject to the unique office and service conditions.
checkedValues./levelChanges/1/changes/0: After at least 3,500,001 XP as Grand Druid, find a successor and abdicate to enter the Hierophant path: reset XP to 1 and relinquish the office-related extra spell levels.

checkedValues./sections/0/description: PHB pp. 32–33 presents combinations operated at the same time by non-human or semi-human characters. The combinations available depend on race; this is a separate procedure from changing professions.
checkedValues./sections/1/description: PHB p. 33’s human-only profession change stops advancement in the former class. It requires principal attribute scores of at least 15 in the original class and 17 or 18 in the new class, with alignment restrictions. The character retains earlier hit points but begins the new class’s other functions at level 1. Former-class functions restrict new-class XP until the new level exceeds the old one.
checkedValues./sections/2/description: The bard appendix supplies a fighter → thief → bard sequence. UA supplies a thief-acrobat specialist path and an advanced druid track with an XP reset. Each follows its own cited transition rules; their labels do not grant general permission to combine classes.
checkedValues./terminologyNotes/0: “Dual-class” is a navigation gloss here. PHB p. 33 heads its sequential rule “The Character With Two Classes.”
checkedValues./terminologyNotes/1: The bard appendix permits humans and half-elves, while the general two-class rule requires a human. The bard guide is classified by its appendix sequence rather than automatically assigned that general procedure.
checkedValues./terminologyNotes/2: For the bard’s thief-stage transition, PHB p. 117 says “between 5th and 9th.” This metadata retains that wording without resolving its boundary convention.
checkedValues./terminologyNotes/3: UA p. 23 calls thief-acrobat a “split-class” specialist; UA p. 25 otherwise treats the specialist as a thief except for the stated changes.

checkedValues./bullets/2: Combat, spellcasting and similar activity do not count as rest.

checkedValues./summary: At 0 hit points a creature becomes unconscious under this DMG procedure, then loses 1 point per following round until death at −10. Immediate aid stops that continuing loss.
checkedValues./bullets/0: The text optionally allows the triggering blow to leave the creature as low as −3.
checkedValues./bullets/1: After revival: 1d6 turns of coma and at least one week of rest; ordinary cures do not remove the restriction, but heal does.
checkedValues./bullets/2: More severe negative totals can have lasting consequences at the DM's option.

checkedValues./summary: The DM weighs the challenge against the participating characters' power before determining XP awards. Outwitting guards and overcoming traps can also qualify.
checkedValues./bullets/0: The award procedure is not simply a fixed reward for every encounter.
checkedValues./bullets/1: Challenge adjustments require referee judgment.

checkedValues./summary: Treasure must be removed from the dungeon or lair and converted to a transportable form or stored safely to count for experience.
checkedValues./bullets/0: Gold-equivalent treasure can award 1 XP per gp when the challenge warrants it; weaker guardians reduce the ratio.
checkedValues./bullets/1: Items sold before XP is awarded contribute their sale proceeds to treasure taken.
checkedValues./bullets/2: Retained magic items receive their smaller listed XP value rather than sale value.

checkedValues./summary: The suggested method divides monster XP equally among surviving participants, with adjustments for challenge and henchman status.
checkedValues./bullets/0: A genuinely single-handed kill can be credited separately.
checkedValues./bullets/1: A caster protected by allies is not acting single-handedly.

checkedValues./summary: Reaching an XP threshold does not automatically grant the next level. The DM assesses performance and the required period of training or study.
checkedValues./bullets/0: The assessment ordinarily determines 1–4 weeks of training.
checkedValues./bullets/1: Below name level, standard weekly cost is the current level × 1,500 gp.
checkedValues./bullets/2: Do not treat the next level's benefits as available before training is completed.

checkedValues./summary: Initial training normally requires a tutor of the same class and profession. A performance score below 2 permits self-training at twice the time.
checkedValues./bullets/0: Name-level self-study and bard contributions have separate rules.
checkedValues./bullets/1: Training must be continuous; serious interruption loses the prior time and payment.
checkedValues./bullets/2: Once eligible to advance, further XP cannot be accumulated until the new level is actually acquired.
checkedValues./bullets/3: Bards contribute at least 50% of monetary gains plus 1,000 gp per level upon advancement to their college, through a druid able to use more of their highest-level spells than the bard; failure to pay prevents advancement. They otherwise need one week of study or training upon gaining sufficient XP.

checkedValues./summary: UA adds comeliness for physical appearance and initial reactions. Charisma still governs the longer-term interpersonal relationship once a character is known.
checkedValues./bullets/0: Charisma and race can adjust effective comeliness.
checkedValues./bullets/1: Extreme scores have special effects; consult the full table before applying them.
checkedValues./bullets/2: The following reaction bands concern creatures of human sort. At −16 or below, viewers recoil, flee or may attack; if viewer and subject are both evil, treat the score as positive. At −15 to −9, viewers show disgust and hostility; if all are evil, the negative score can be regarded as positive. At −8 to 0, viewers feel aversion and may become openly hostile.
checkedValues./bullets/3: At 1–6, viewers tend toward unease; enough conversation can let charisma offset it. At 7–9, the initial reaction is negative but high charisma can quickly overcome it. At 10–13, appearance has no effect on the viewer.
checkedValues./bullets/4: At 14–17, initial reaction improves by a percentage equal to the score; members of the opposite sex are affected as by fascination unless their Wisdom exceeds half the score.
checkedValues./bullets/5: At 18–21, initial reaction improves by 150% of the score. Opposite-sex viewers are affected as by fascination unless Wisdom exceeds two-thirds the score; same-sex viewers are similarly affected unless Wisdom is at least half the score. Harsh rejection can cause the rejected individual to react as if the subject had negative comeliness equal to half the positive score.
checkedValues./bullets/6: At 22–25, the reaction adjustment is twice the score. Fascination affects those with Wisdom less than two-thirds of the score; a consciously sought opposite-sex individual is fascinated unless Wisdom is 18 or higher. Harsh rejection has the same effect as in the 18–21 band.
checkedValues./bullets/7: At 26–30, reserved for unusual extraplanar demigods or deities, the reaction adjustment is twice the score. Fascination applies except to those with Wisdom at least 75% of the score, and Wisdom 19 or higher always permits a saving throw. A consciously sought opposite-sex individual is affected unless Wisdom is 20 or higher.
checkedValues./bullets/8: Fascination allows a saving throw versus spell; nonmagical comeliness fascination is not removed by dispel magic or antimagic. A fascinated creature follows an order if 3d6 does not exceed the subject’s comeliness: add 1 to the roll for requests against its interest, up to +6 or more for hazardous requests; a higher roll breaks fascination. Treatment during fascination affects subsequent reaction.
checkedValues./bullets/9: Comeliness is temporary as a reaction factor: once the subject is known, use charisma. Fascination does not prevent fighting or spellcasting or make the subject a puppet. Change self and alter self adjust comeliness by at most 1 point; an illusion of a high-comeliness creature works for one round; polymorph changes it by 2 points; shapechange gives the final form’s full effect.

checkedValues./notes/0: This is a partial transcription of matrix I.B, not a reconstructed full table. Every null cell is unavailable from the current OCR and must be checked in the original scan.
checkedValues./notes/1: The table applies to fighters, paladins, and rangers. Bards use their highest attained fighter level, not their current bard level. Its separate level-0 column applies to halflings and humans.
checkedValues./notes/2: A cell is the table's 20-sided-die target for the named attacker level band and opponent armor class, before resolving applicable adjustments. It is not automatically equivalent to AC-zero target minus armor class.
checkedValues./notes/3: The original table repeats 20 in some columns, so a single linear THAC0 subtraction can disagree with it. The examples below use only cells actually legible in this scan.
checkedValues./ruleNotes/0/text: The matrix prints a −2 adjustment at medium missile range and −5 at long range.
checkedValues./ruleNotes/1/text: The DM may choose a +1 to-hit bonus at the second level within each two-level fighter band, producing the source's optional per-level progression instead of the ordinary two-level steps. Do not silently apply this option.
checkedValues./ruleNotes/2/text: For the listed kinds of spell effects, including curse, prayer, and protection from evil, the DMG instructs the referee to adjust the relevant armor class rather than reduce the attack die result. This preserves the intended repeated-20 behavior. This note is about those spell adjustments, not a universal conversion of every modifier into AC.
checkedValues./ruleNotes/3/text: The DMG explains the repeated 20s as part of the printed combat-table progression. It then offers an optional amendment: second and later repeated-20 entries require a natural 20, and targets above 20 require a natural 20 plus sufficient bonus. The initial 20 entry still permits die result plus bonuses. Keep that amendment distinct from the unamended printed table; do not infer an unconditional natural-20 rule from it.
checkedValues./comparisonExamples/0/explanation: With no additional adjustments in this illustration, the original matrix's repeated 20 differs from the linear calculation 20 − (−1).
checkedValues./comparisonExamples/1/explanation: The source-listed cell is 20; a simple AC-zero subtraction would produce 24. No missing cells were generated from that formula.
